title: Virtual Machine Scale Sets and autoscale
learningObjective: Create a scale set with the right orchestration mode and upgrade policy. Write autoscale rules that add and remove VMs without bouncing up and down.
foundation: A Virtual Machine Scale Set manages a group of VMs as one unit, so you can run many identical web servers and add or remove them automatically.
Autoscale watches a metric such as CPU and adds instances when it is high and removes them when it is low, within a minimum and maximum you set.
Scale sets can spread instances across availability zones and fault domains for resilience.
engineer: Orchestration modes: Flexible, recommended, where instances are normal VMs, can mix sizes, can be managed with VM commands, and are spread across fault domains and zones; Uniform, where instances are identical copies of one model, managed with scale set (VMSS) commands, good for very large stateless fleets.

Upgrade policy (what happens when you change the model, for example a new image): Manual, where you upgrade instances yourself; Automatic, where all instances update in any order, maybe all at once; Rolling, where instances update in batches with pauses and health checks (Application Health extension or a load balancer probe).
Autoscale profile: a minimum, a maximum and a default number of instances.

Autoscale rule: which metric (for example CPU); how to average it; the condition and threshold (for example > 70%); how long to look back (for example 10 minutes); what to do (add or remove a number or percent); the cooldown, how long to wait before the next change (default 5 minutes).
Scheduled profiles: change the minimum and maximum for peaks you know about, such as a sale day.
How autoscale decides: it adds instances if any scale-out rule is true. It removes instances only when the scale-in rule is true.

Avoiding bouncing (flapping): before removing instances, autoscale estimates the new load. If that would trigger a scale-out straight away, it skips the scale-in. Keep a gap between thresholds, for example out above 70% and in below 30%.
Which VMs are removed (scale-in policy): Default, which keeps zones and fault domains balanced, then removes the highest instance ID; NewestVM; OldestVM.
Instance protection: stops specific instances from being removed or upgraded.
Setting up instances: use custom images from Azure Compute Gallery, and cloud-init or extensions for configuration.
Limits: up to 1,000 VMs in a scale set (sometimes fewer with custom images). Autoscale needs metric data; guest OS metrics need the Azure Monitor agent.

animation.caption: Tune VMSS autoscale rules against a traffic peak and watch instances follow.

example.title: The web shop on Black Friday
body: The shop's web tier is a Flexible scale set across three zones. Autoscale keeps 3 to 30 instances. It adds 2 when average CPU is above 70% for 10 minutes, and removes 1 when it's below 30% for 15 minutes. Cooldown is 5 minutes.
A scheduled profile raises the minimum to 10 on the sale day. Rolling upgrades with health probes roll out a patched image with no downtime.

prerequisites: A VNet and subnet, and a load balancer or Application Gateway
An image (from the Marketplace or Compute Gallery)
permissions: Monitoring Contributor, to edit autoscale settings
portal: Virtual machine scale sets > Create: orchestration mode, image, size, zones, scaling (manual or autoscale), upgrade policy, health monitoring.
Scale set > Scaling: Custom autoscale > add rules and schedule profiles; view run history.
Scale set > Instances: upgrade, protect or delete instances.
configuration.cli:
az vmss create -g rg-app -n vmss-web --image Ubuntu2204 --orchestration-mode Flexible --vm-sku Standard_D2s_v5 \
  --instance-count 2 --zones 1 2 3 --admin-username azureuser --generate-ssh-keys
az monitor autoscale create -g rg-app --resource vmss-web --resource-type Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachineScaleSets \
  --name as-web --min-count 2 --max-count 10 --count 2
az monitor autoscale rule create -g rg-app --autoscale-name as-web --condition "Percentage CPU > 70 avg 10m" --scale out 1
az monitor autoscale rule create -g rg-app --autoscale-name as-web --condition "Percentage CPU < 30 avg 10m" --scale in 1
az vmss scale -g rg-app -n vmss-web --new-capacity 5
configuration.powershell:
New-AzVmss -ResourceGroupName rg-app -VMScaleSetName vmss-web -Location westeurope -OrchestrationMode Flexible -VmSize Standard_D2s_v5 `
  -InstanceCount 2 -Zone 1,2,3 -ImageName Ubuntu2204 -Credential (Get-Credential)
Update-AzVmss -ResourceGroupName rg-app -VMScaleSetName vmss-web -SkuCapacity 5
Get-AzAutoscaleSetting -ResourceGroupName rg-app

lab.objective: Design autoscale rules that handle a peak without flapping or saturation.
steps: Run the default rules and read the instance curve.
Apply 'Flapping' and 'Max too low' presets and explain each warning.
Find settings that keep CPU unsaturated with the fewest scale actions.

validation.text: Tuned autoscale to a healthy result

lab.cost: None. The simulation runs entirely in the browser.

troubleshooting.cause: The scale-in threshold is too low, or flapping protection blocks it.
troubleshooting.fix: Widen the gap between thresholds, and check the autoscale run history.

troubleshooting.cause: The metric isn't available (for example guest metrics without the agent), or the profile is turned off.
troubleshooting.fix: Check the run history and whether the metric has data.

troubleshooting.symptom: A model change didn't reach the instances.
troubleshooting.fix: Upgrade the instances, or switch to Rolling.

troubleshooting.symptom: New instances fail health checks during a rolling upgrade.
troubleshooting.cause: A bad image or app setting.
troubleshooting.fix: The rolling upgrade pauses. Fix the image and resume.

comparisons.difference: The same idea, with launch templates and scaling policies.
The same Azure Monitor autoscale engine, used for App Service plans.

misconceptions.reality: No. It looks at the metric over the look-back window, and waits for the cooldown.

misconceptions.myth: You need Uniform mode for autoscale.
misconceptions.reality: No. Both modes support autoscale. Flexible is recommended for new deployments.

architectureDecisions: Flexible mode across zones: the default choice for new scale sets.
Metric rules plus schedules: schedules handle the peaks you know about, metrics handle the rest.
Rolling upgrades with health probes: a bad image stops after the first batch.

walkthrough.subtitle: Run many identical VMs that grow and shrink with demand.

steps.label: Busy evenings
steps.title: Traffic triples every evening
body: Two VMs are too few at 8 p.m. and too many at 4 a.m. Adding VMs by hand every day is not a plan.

steps.label: Scale set
steps.title: A scale set manages identical VMs as one
body: A Virtual Machine Scale Set creates instances from one configuration and spreads them across fault domains or zones. Put it behind a load balancer.
Flexible orchestration (the default) lets you mix sizes and manage instances like normal VMs; Uniform uses identical instances managed only through the set.

steps.label: Autoscale
steps.title: Autoscale adds and removes instances
body: Set a minimum, maximum and default instance count. Add rules: scale out by 1 when average CPU is over 70% for 10 minutes; scale in by 1 when under 30%. Or scale on a schedule.

callout.text: Always add a scale-in rule too, or the set only ever grows.

steps.label: Upgrades
steps.title: Updating the instances
body: The upgrade policy decides how model changes reach instances: Manual (you upgrade each), Automatic (all at once), or Rolling (in batches, safest).

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: Scale sets
body: Many identical VMs, sized by demand.
recap: One config, many instances, behind a load balancer
Min, max, default + scale out AND scale in rules

handsOn.title: Create a small scale set with an autoscale rule
handsOn.cost: Low. Two B1s instances cost about US$0.02 per hour together. Delete the same day.
before: Signed in at portal.azure.com as Owner of a subscription (a free or pay-as-you-go account works). Work in a resource group called rg-az104-lab.
If rg-az104-lab does not exist yet: search 'Resource groups' > Create > name rg-az104-lab, region UAE North (or any region near you) > Review + create > Create.

steps.do: Search 'Virtual machine scale sets' > + Create. Group rg-az104-lab, name vmss-lab, region your region, orchestration: Flexible, image Ubuntu 24.04, size Standard_B1s, password authentication.
Scaling section: choose Autoscaling, then 'Configure'. Default 2, minimum 1, maximum 3. Scale out: CPU above 70% adds 1. Scale in: CPU below 30% removes 1. Save.
steps.see: A summary of the scaling policy.

steps.do: Networking tab: keep the new VNet. Do not add a load balancer for this lab. Review + create > Create.
steps.see: Deployment completes in a few minutes.
Your autoscale settings: minimum 1, maximum 3, default 2, and both rules.

steps.do: Wait about 15 minutes, then open Scaling > Run history (or Instances).
steps.see: CPU stays under 30%, so the scale-in rule removes one instance, down to the minimum of 1.
steps.tip: The default count is only used when metrics are unavailable; the rules decide the real count.

steps.see: The upgrade mode for model changes.

check: The scale set has instances and an autoscale profile with scale-out and scale-in rules.
cleanup: When you finish for the day: Resource groups > rg-az104-lab > Delete resource group > type the name > Delete. This removes everything inside it.
